narrative:
The 2022 Cincinnati Reds were a team in transition and in trouble, stumbling out of the gate with a dreadful 3-18 April that immediately signaled this would be a long, painful rebuild. The pitching staff was a revolving door of misfortune, with relievers Art Warren, Joel Kuhnel, and Hunter Strickland repeatedly coughing up leads and surrendering crushing home runs at the worst possible moments. An offense that ranked among the league's worst — posting a collective .676 OPS — gave their battered bullpen almost no margin for error, and the early months exposed just how thin the roster truly was.

A brief flicker of hope arrived in May and July, when the Reds pieced together winning records and showed flashes of what their young core could become. Jonathan India's clutch walk-off single in mid-July and Brandon Drury's timely two-RBI hit offered glimpses of competitiveness, moments that reminded Cincinnati fans there were players worth watching even amid the wreckage. But these bright spots were islands in a sea of struggle, never sustained long enough to shift the season's direction.

August brought more of the same contradictions: TJ Friedl delivered a thrilling triple that briefly ignited hope, only for Alexis Díaz — a young reliever showing both promise and growing pains — to surrender a crushing double that erased the lead the very same game. The bullpen's inconsistency was maddening, and a team that could never quite string together enough wins fell further and further from any postseason conversation.

By September and October, the Reds were playing out the string, finishing 62-100 and allowing 815 runs on the year. The season's final chapter was a quiet, forgettable collapse, ending with Kevin Newman singling home a run against a Cincinnati team that had long since packed away its playoff dreams. The 2022 Reds were a cautionary tale of rebuilding done painfully slowly, with a bullpen that cost them countless close games and an offense that rarely gave them a fighting chance.

chapters.title: Disaster from the Start
chapters.description: A historically bad April sets the tone as Cincinnati's bullpen implodes and the team loses 18 of its first 21 games.

chapters.title: A Glimmer of Competitiveness
chapters.description: The Reds post a winning May and a strong July, with India and Drury delivering clutch hits that hint at the team's potential.

chapters.title: Midsummer Meltdown
chapters.description: Just as momentum builds, opposing hitters punish a shaky bullpen through July and into early August, erasing any gains.

chapters.title: Fleeting Bright Spots
chapters.description: August produces Friedl's electric triple and Barrero's clutch single, but Díaz surrenders a devastating double in the same game, summing up the Reds' maddening inconsistency.

chapters.title: Playing Out the String
chapters.description: September and October bring a 9-19 and 2-3 finish as Cincinnati surrenders the season's final meaningful plays to opponents and closes out a 62-100 campaign.
